Newton’s second law (non-relativistic, constant mass) states:
- F = m a (vector form: the force on an object equals its mass times its acceleration; F and a point in the same direction; m is a scalar).

More generally:
- F = dp/dt, where p = m v. If mass is not constant, F = d(mv)/dt = m a + v (dm/dt).

Explanation of the multiplicative-combination substrate:
- The law is a multiplicative relationship: force is the product of two core ingredients—mass (the object's inertia) and acceleration (the rate of change of velocity). Mass sets how strongly a given acceleration affects the force; acceleration sets how quickly velocity changes.
- Magnitude-wise, |F| ∝ m |a|, so doubling mass (at the same acceleration) doubles the force, and doubling acceleration (at the same mass) also doubles the force.
- Direction-wise, F points in the same direction as a (for constant mass).
- If mass varies with time, the full relation F = d(mv)/dt introduces an additional term (v dm/dt), but the underlying multiplicative idea—mass scales the effect of motion change on force—still underlies the relation.

In short: Newton’s second law is the product of inertia (mass) and the rate of change of motion (acceleration), which is why it fits the multiplicative-combination substrate.
